core_obligations: Easy direction: if A is tensor independent from B over C with C contained in a model, then A forks independently from B over C, because the type of A over CB extends to a C-invariant global type (proof lines 1111-1112).

Reduction: assuming A forks independently from B over C, replace C by acl(BC) so that C is contained in B and B is algebraically closed, and suppose for a contradiction that A is not tensor independent (proof lines 1113-1115).

The continuation of the proof is the author's own claim: with A' = acl(AC) and a C-indiscernible sequence of copies of B, the sequence is tensor-dependent at each step; this claim is stated and then proved inside the counted spans, and the main proof is closed by it (proof span 1124-1128 for the claim, 1133-1169 for its proof, which splits into the two cases of the definition of tensor independence and uses that A' is a model by the cited lemma).
proof_roadmap: Settle the easy direction through invariant global types (proof lines 1111-1112).
Reduce to algebraically closed B containing C, state the author's claim about the indiscernible sequence, and prove it case by case (proof spans 1113-1169).
difficulty_reason: The lemma identifies two independence relations in the r-space theories of the paper: forking independence over C and tensor independence, the latter being free amalgamation of the algebraic closures (statement lines 1089-1091). The proof disposes of one direction through invariant global types and reduces the other to the case where C is contained in an algebraically closed B, then finishes by the author's own claim about a C-indiscernible sequence of copies of B (proof lines 1111-1115 and the claim at 1124-1128). The step that carries the content is the proof of that claim, which splits according to the two ways tensor dependence can fail - either the algebraic closure is not larger than the union, or it is strictly larger - and in each case exhibits a finite set of neighbours witnessing the dependence of the next copy (proof lines 1133-1169). The author explicitly closes the main proof by pointing at the claim, so the claim and its proof are counted as the continuation of the same proof. H2.
